newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government uses phone-taps, increasingly.
newsitem.headline: French government uses phone-taps, increasingly.

text.p: France's government is resorting increasingly to phone-taps, and pays ever less heed to its advice, the National Commission for Control of Intercepts and Security (CNCIS) said on Thursday.

The CNCIS said in its annual report that for the first time in five years, it had authorised the government this year to increase the number of phonelines which can be tapped simultaneously from 1,180 to 1,540.

The reason for this was "the increase in the number of lines, particularly mobile phones, which totals more than 32 million, and the decision to allocate a contingent to the gendarmerie (paramilitary police).
In 1996, a total of 4,603 phone lines were tapped against 4,492 the previous year, CNCIS president Paul Bouchet told a news conference.
The government dropped 20 requests following negative advice from the commission, against 40 the previous year. But in six cases the government overrode the commission -- against three cases in 1995.

Under a 1991 law, phone taps can be carried out for the police and the gendarmerie only on grounds of national security, safeguarding economic or scientific interests, and the fight against crime or terrorism.
The report was published just two days after the CNCIS handed it to Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has pledged to stamp out illegal wiretaps.
Bouchet acknowledged it was easy to circumvert controls and reiterated his denunciation of clandestine telephone taps by private groups, estimated at some 100,000.

"We trust the police of the (French) republic but we know some individuals can be dishonest. In private firms, there are former police officers and they are not the ones who have honoured that institution," Bouchet said.
He suggested that public prosecutors investigate companies which trade in equipment used to tap phones, and called for tougher controls on such firms and higher penalties for illegal taps.

Under a bill to be debated by the Senate next month, the maximum sentence for illegal taps would be doubled to two years. The commission would be given the task of monitoring the 4,741 companies dealing in investigations and security, and using or trading in equipment which could be used for taps.
Bouchet published his report days after new revelations of wire-tapping under the rule of former President Francois Mitterrand.

Files of Mitterrand's former anti-terrorist cell, extracts of which were published by the media, show he personally oversaw widespread illegal taps of journalists, lawyers and politicians. Many papers carried his handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).
Bouchet was this week directed to study documents from Mitterrand's since-disbanded cell seized by the DST counter- intelligence service last month on national security grounds.
He will report back to Juppe within a few weeks on whether their seizure was justified.
French media have reported that up to 2,000 people were victims of wiretapping by the Elysee palace unit. The daily Liberation said some 100,000 people were being illegally wiretapped each year.
